findings.detail: The auditor cannot provide full assurance over 2025/26 opening balances (especially property, plant and equipment) or closing reserves. findings.paper_title: Appendix A – BCP Council - Regaining assurance progress report and sector update
findings.headline: Four consecutive years without a clean audit opinion, with no improvement expected for 2025/26
findings.detail: The council received audit disclaimers for 2022/23, 2023/24, and 2024/25. For 2025/26, the auditor explicitly states they do not expect to issue an unqualified opinion because they lack sufficient assurance over opening balances from the prior-year disclaimers. This is a four-year run of failed audit opinions.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director needs verified financial statements to assess creditworthiness. Four years of qualified audit opinions—with no resolution in sight—means the council's true financial position cannot be independently verified.
findings.figures: Disclaimers issued for 2022/23, 2023/24, 2024/25; no unqualified opinion expected for 2025/26
findings.quote: As a result of the disclaimer of opinion issued for the previous three financial years, and a lack of assurance over opening balances for the previous audit year we do not expect to be able to undertake sufficient work to support an unmodified audit opinion on the 2025/26 financial statements in advance of the backstop date.

findings.matters: An extended multi-year audit remediation period means the council will remain in non-compliant status for years, extending the period of elevated credit risk and regulatory scrutiny.

findings.paper_title: Annual Breaches of Financial Regulations and Procurement Decision Records Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Emergency housing has been spot-purchased without procurement processes for years, creating a £15.7m uncontrolled expenditure stream
findings.detail: The council spot-purchased B&B and hotel accommodation for emergency homeless provisions (primarily Premier Inn and Travelodge) without any PDRs or procurement involvement. This practice originated in legacy councils and continued despite Financial Regulations from 2022/23 requiring PDRs. An internal audit found that no PDRs had ever been completed for this expenditure. The council has now created a 15-month PDR and plans a long-term procurement strategy with quarterly oversight.
findings.matters: A £15.7m demand-driven service with no prior procurement controls represents both a historical governance failure and an ongoing budget vulnerability; lack of competitive process raises value-for-money concerns.

Management wrongly assumed Cabinet and Council approval made PDR unnecessary. This breach was identified during the 2025/26 Housing Acquisitions Audit, alongside multiple other large housing breaches (£1.035m, £500k, £56k, £35k, £31k), indicating systemic rather than isolated control failures in this directorate.
findings.matters: Large capital housing schemes without proper procurement oversight represent a material control weakness; the pattern suggests prior housing decisions may also lack documentation, creating audit and challenge risk for the council.

findings.quote: Procurement was involved with the pre-construction phase of residential construction of 110 homes and a PDR of £513,610 was approved. However, Procurement was not involved in the actual construction phase and there was no PDR approval for this phase.

This is a result of increasing demand and in response to the improvements required to address the statutory SEND directive

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – External Auditor – Auditor’s Annual Report Year ending 31 March 2025 (Final)
findings.headline: Cashflow impact of £4.7m in 2024/25 rising to £7.5m in 2025/26; capitalisation directive rejected by government
findings.detail: The council estimated a £4.7m cashflow cost in 2024/25 from the DSG deficit, rising to £7.5m in 2025/26. The council applied for a capitalisation directive to cover the DSG deficit but this was rejected. Instead, MHCLG agreed a temporary increase in borrowing capacity within treasury management powers.
findings.matters: The sustained annual cashflow drain and rejection of a capitalisation directive means the council must rely on temporary borrowing arrangements with no permanent solution, creating ongoing liquidity pressure.
findings.figures: £4.7m cashflow impact 2024/25; £7.5m estimated 2025/26
findings.quote: The cashflow impact is estimated to be in the region of £4.7m in 2024/25 and a further £7.5m in 2025/26. In order to manage this impact, the Council applied for a capitalisation directive to cover the £DSG deficit in 25/26. This was rejected but the MHCLG agreed an increase in their temporary borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – External Auditor – Auditor’s Annual Report Year ending 31 March 2025 (Final)
findings.headline: Short-term borrowing nearly tripled in one year to £121.5m to manage cashflow crisis from DSG deficit
findings.detail: Short-term borrowing increased from £43.5m at 31 March 2024 to £121.5m at 31 March 2025 - a 179% increase. This borrowing was taken specifically to fund cashflow issues resulting from the DSG deficit. Long-term borrowing also increased from £294.8m to £371.0m. The council has been given permission to exceed its Capital Finance Requirements in 2025/26 but has not yet done so.
findings.matters: The rapid escalation of short-term borrowing indicates the council is using emergency measures to manage cashflow; this is unsustainable and signals potential inability to service debt.
findings.figures: Short-term borrowing: £43.5m (31 March 2024) to £121.5m (31 March 2025); long-term borrowing: £294.8m to £371.0m
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2024, the Council had short-term borrowings of £43.5m. By 31 March 2025, this had increased to £121.5m, whereas long term borrowing was £294.8m as at 31 March 2024 and £371.0m as at 31 March 2025. Short-term borrowing increased in 2024/25 to fund the cashflow issues resulting from the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) cumulative deficit.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – External Auditor – Auditor’s Annual Report Year ending 31 March 2025 (Final)
findings.headline: DSG cumulative deficit expanding rapidly to £180m by end of 2025/26, identified as significant weakness
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant deficit was £113.3m at 31 March 2025 and is forecast to reach £180m by end of 2025/26. Usable reserves at £87m are considerably below this cumulative deficit. The council lacks sufficient reserves should the statutory override be removed. This is the most significant financial pressure identified.
findings.matters: A £180m deficit growing faster than reserve capacity directly threatens the council's financial sustainability and signals potential future insolvency if government support is withdrawn.
findings.figures: £113.3m at 31 March 2025; £180.0m projected at end of 2025/26; usable reserves £87.0m (£27.3m general fund, £55.7m earmarked)
findings.quote: The Council remains under significant financial pressure and is not financially sustainable. Its Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) cumulative deficit continued to significantly increase in 2024/25 to £113.3m and is expected to be £180m at the end of 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – External Auditor – Auditor’s Annual Report Year ending 31 March 2025 (Final)
findings.headline: Disclaimer opinion issued on financial statements due to insufficient audit evidence
findings.detail: The auditor could not obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence over the council's in-year movements of net pension liability, property plant and equipment, and closing reserves. This resulted in a disclaimer opinion being issued on 27 January 2026, which is the most serious type of audit opinion.
findings.matters: A disclaimer opinion signals the auditor cannot confirm the financial statements are accurate; this creates significant uncertainty about the council's true financial position and is material to any lending decision.
findings.figures: Disclaimer opinion issued 27 January 2026
findings.quote: Due to the impact of the Local Government Backstop on the 2022/23 financial statements, we have issued a disclaimer opinion on 2025/26 financial statements as a result of being unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence over the Council's in year movements of the net pension liability and property plant and equipment and the closing balance of property, plant and equipment and closing reserves.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Audit Findings Reports 2024-25
findings.headline: Heritage assets revaluation error of £6.96m at Russell Cotes group charity requires adjustment
findings.detail: Audit review of heritage assets held by Russell Cotes Art Gallery and Museum Charitable Trust (a material group entity) identified an error in the revaluation adjustment that overstated the heritage asset value by £6.96m. This was corrected in the final group accounts.
findings.matters: Material adjustment required at group level; indicates valuation control weaknesses; heritage assets are revalued annually creating ongoing risk of material misstatement.
findings.figures: Heritage assets adjustment: £6.96m reduction at group level
findings.quote: Our review of heritage assets identified an adjustment to the valuation of heritage assets, reducing the value by £6.96m due to the revaluation adjustment being incorrect.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Audit Findings Reports 2024-25
findings.headline: Significant audit delays in housing benefit expenditure working papers and new IT system implementation
findings.detail: The auditor identified significant delays in obtaining working papers to support the audit of housing benefit expenditure, which cascaded into delays completing the IT review of the new housing benefit system implementation. While the council has improved response times and allocated additional resources, these delays persist and indicate ongoing control and governance issues.
findings.matters: Housing benefit is material expenditure; new system implementation delays suggest control weaknesses; persistent audit access delays indicate weak governance and internal control environment.
findings.figures: Housing benefit system: new implementation with outstanding audit completion work
findings.quote: However, we identified significant delays in obtaining working papers to support audit of housing benefit expenditure which also impacted the completion of our IT review of the new system implementation.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Audit Findings Reports 2024-25
findings.headline: Unadjusted property valuation errors of £5.7m in land and buildings with new valuer
findings.detail: Testing of a sample of land and buildings valuations (which total £857.58m, up £54m from prior year) identified calculation errors on two assets overstating values by £5.7m. Management has not adjusted these errors, reporting them as unadjusted misstatements. The Council used a new external valuer (Lambert Smith Hampton) for the 2024/25 five-yearly revaluation cycle.
findings.matters: Unadjusted errors suggest either weak control over the valuation process or incomplete asset records; material increase in valuations combined with new valuer creates risk of further undetected overstatement.
findings.figures: Unadjusted errors: £5.7m; total land and buildings: £857.58m (increase of £54m from £803.54m prior year)
findings.quote: Two assets which were selected for testing were identified to have errors in the calculations of the valuations which overstated the valuations by £5.7m in total. Management has not adjusted for these areas on the basis of materiality and these are reported as unadjusted errors.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Audit Findings Reports 2024-25
findings.headline: Pension net position reversed to £62.88m liability following asset ceiling correction affecting first-time application
findings.detail: The council initially reported a pension net asset of £66.15m in draft accounts, but correction of a missed IFRIC 14 asset ceiling requirement (not applied by the actuary) resulted in a net liability of £62.88m. This is the first year the asset ceiling applies, following years of reducing net defined benefit liabilities. The £128.07m asset ceiling adjustment represents a material reversal of the pension position.
findings.matters: Material swing of £128m in pension position; indicates pension fund has recovered sufficiently to trigger asset ceiling constraints; continuing reduction in net liabilities suggests long-term deterioration in funded status.
findings.figures: Draft pension net asset: £66.15m; final pension net liability: £62.88m; asset ceiling: £128.07m
findings.quote: In the 2024/25 draft accounts, the Council reported a pension net asset position of £66.15m... On receipt of the updated report, the actuary applied a £128.07m asset ceiling which has resulted in an overall net position for the Council balance sheet of a net liability of £62.88m. This is the first year which the Council has been required to apply an asset ceiling due to the continuing reduction in the net defined liability position over recent years to an asset position in 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Audit Findings Reports 2024-25
findings.headline: Significant Value for Money weaknesses in schools grant deficit and SEND statutory direction
findings.detail: The auditor has identified significant weaknesses in the council's arrangements for economy, efficiency and effectiveness in two specific areas: the dedicated schools grant (DSG) deficit and special education needs and disabilities (SEND), where a statutory direction from government is already in place. These findings indicate operational and financial control failures in these areas.
findings.matters: Significant VFM weaknesses mean government regulators or intervention may follow; DSG deficit represents a structural financial problem with no immediate solution; SEND statutory direction indicates the council is already operating under government constraint.
findings.figures: DSG deficit and SEND statutory direction both identified as areas of significant weakness
findings.quote: We identified significant weaknesses in the Authority's arrangements and so are not satisfied that the Authority has made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources in relation to the dedicates schools grant deficit and the statutory direction in place in relation to SEND (special education needs and disabilities).

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Audit Findings Reports 2024-25
findings.headline: Auditor unable to form an opinion on the financial statements due to prior year backstop audit limitations
findings.detail: The auditor cannot issue an unmodified audit opinion on the 2024/25 financial statements. This follows a 2022/23 backstop disclaimed opinion, which has left the auditor without sufficient assurance over opening balances. The audit will not be formally certified before the 27 February 2026 backstop deadline.
findings.matters: Lenders cannot rely on an independently verified financial position; the council's finance directors cannot certify that accounts are fairly stated. This is a fundamental reporting failure with no external validation.
findings.figures: Backstop deadline: 27 February 2026; prior year (2022/23) disclaimed opinion carries forward
findings.quote: Owing to the challenges of undertaking an audit where a previous years' audit (2022/23) was subject to backstop-related disclaimed audit opinion, we have been unable to undertake sufficient work to support an unmodified audit opinion in advance of the backstop date of 27 February 2026. The limitations imposed by not having assurance on opening balances mean that we will be unable to form an opinion on the financial statements.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Monitoring report for the period April to December 2025 and Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Treasury surplus and borrowing strategy dependent on sustained favorable market conditions; will reverse when rates normalize
findings.detail: The £1.1m forecast surplus is entirely driven by lower PWLB borrowing rates (£0.6m saving) and higher-than-expected investment returns (4.16% vs 4.05% SONIA benchmark). The council's strategy of borrowing cash into April 2026 to maximize investment returns depends on these conditions persisting. When Bank of England rates stabilize at expected 3.5% mid-2026, both investment income and borrowing savings will decline.
findings.matters: Lenders should understand the council's current financial headroom is temporary, supported by market tailwinds; the structural deficit remains and will become more acute when rates normalize.
findings.figures: £1.1m forecast surplus (vs £0.3m at Q2), £0.6m from PWLB rate savings, investment returns 4.16% vs benchmark 4.05%, Bank of England rate expected to stabilize at 3.5% during middle of 2026
findings.quote: The reason for this improved forecast is primarily due to greater availability of funds within the local authority market than expected and at rates lower now than forecast at Q2.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Monitoring report for the period April to December 2025 and Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Accumulated deficit driving significant short-term borrowing increases since April 2022
findings.detail: Short-term debt has increased substantially to fund the cash demand of an accumulated deficit, overlaid in Table 6 chart as accumulated DSG deficit. Rather than drawing down reserves, the council is funding this through ongoing short-term borrowing, indicating the deficit is structural.
findings.matters: Lenders must distinguish cyclical from structural debt; funding ongoing deficits through continuous borrowing is unsustainable and signals unresolved spending/income gaps that could pressure service delivery or reserves.
findings.figures: Short-term borrowing increased significantly since April 2022; specific DSG deficit amount not quantified in report
findings.quote: Debts in the short term have increased significantly to satisfy the cash demand of the deficit.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 10 - s25 CFO Reserves Strategy Report 202627
findings.headline: Fair Pay Agreement in Adult Social Care: £4.9m pressure from 2028/29 if care worker pay rises 5.1%, dependent on government grant
findings.detail: New legislation requires a Fair Pay Agreement in Adult Social Care. Government proposes devolving £500m grant nationally in 2028/29 to fund it. One illustrative outcome suggests 5.1% care worker pay increase in April 2028. For BCP Council, this scenario creates £4.9m additional pressure in 2028/29. However, detail on the actual agreement and funding distribution is absent; whether the grant will fully cover costs is unknown.
findings.matters: This is a new structural cost arriving when the DSG crisis is at its peak (2028/29). If the government grant is insufficient, the council will absorb additional social care costs it cannot afford.
findings.figures: National grant devolving: £500m (2028/29). Illustrative care worker pay increase: 5.1% (April 2028). BCP impact (illustrative): £4.9m additional pressure.
findings.quote: One of the illustrative potential outcomes suggests an increase in basic pay to care workers by 5.1% in April 2028. For BCP Council such increase would mean a pressure of £4.9 million in addition to already reported MTFP growth.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 10 - s25 CFO Reserves Strategy Report 202627
findings.headline: Section 117 Mental Health Accommodation: potential £2.4m backpay liability for up to 110 people plus £396k ongoing pressure
findings.detail: Legal guidance confirmed councils must fund specialist accommodation costs for Section 117 aftercare recipients, not the individuals themselves. Up to 110 people in BCP Council may be entitled to back pay up to 6 years old. Potential liability after NHS Dorset contribution could be £2.4m in arrears plus £396k annual ongoing pressure. Current provision of £1.052m may be insufficient.
findings.matters: This is a contingent liability that could crystallise rapidly. The council has no control over the final amount and faces both historic and ongoing costs.
findings.figures: Affected people: up to 110. Potential backpay (after NHS share): £2.4m. Ongoing pressure: £396k annually. Current provision: £1.052m. Service users in 2025/26: ~60.
findings.quote: BCP potential risk after NHS Dorset contribution could be as high as £2.4m in backpay and over £396,000 as an ongoing net pressure.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 10 - s25 CFO Reserves Strategy Report 202627
findings.headline: Children's Services budget doubled since 2019/20; LAC up 19.4%, EHCP numbers doubled to 4,921
findings.detail: Children's Services budget has increased 100% between 2019/20 and 2026/27. Looked After Children increased 19.4% (from 526 in March 2020 to 628 by December 2025). EHCP numbers more than doubled (from 2,448 in January 2020 to 4,921 by November 2025, a 101% increase). Home to School Transport costs £19.3m in 2026/27, an increase of £2.2m on prior year.
findings.matters: Demand growth is outpacing budget growth. A 100% budget increase over five years while still overspending indicates structural demand pressures beyond the council's control.
findings.figures: Children's Services: 100% budget increase 2019/20–2026/27. LAC: 526 (Mar 2020) → 628 (Dec 2025) = 19.4% increase. EHCP: 2,448 (Jan 2020) → 4,921 (Nov 2025) = 101% increase. Home to School Transport: £19.3m (2026/27); £2.2m increase from prior year.
findings.quote: the council continues to face spiralling costs and pressures in children's services which has seen the services budget increase by 100% between 2019/20 and 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 10 - s25 CFO Reserves Strategy Report 202627
findings.headline: Pay award budget of 2.8% is at high risk; council has consistently underprovided for pay settlements
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget assumes 2.8% pay award. Trade unions have claimed £3,000 or 10% (whichever greater); government's indicative position is 2.5%; peer councils assume ~3%. The council has repeatedly underprovided: 2024/25 budgeted 4.5% but paid ~4%, and 2025/26 budgeted 2.8% but settled at 3.2%. Any 1% variance above 2.8% costs £2m, forcing either service cuts or reserve drawdown mid-year.
findings.matters: If the pay award exceeds 2.8%, the council has no room to absorb it within existing budgets given other pressures. Historical underprovision suggests 2.8% is optimistic.
findings.figures: Budget assumption: 2.8%. Union claim: £3,000 or 10% (whichever greater). Government position: 2.5%. Peer councils: ~3% (southwest average). Cost per 1% variance: £2m. Prior settlements: 2024/25 budgeted 4.5%/paid ~4%; 2025/26 budgeted 2.8%/paid 3.2%.
findings.quote: The adequacy or otherwise of the 2.8% provision presents a clear risk to adequacy of the budget.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 10 - s25 CFO Reserves Strategy Report 202627
findings.headline: New pay structure adds £4.5m costs; incremental drift exposure tripled from £1.5m to £4m annually
findings.detail: Council approved a new pay and grading structure in July 2025 adding £4.545m (2.44% increase on pay base), which was £1.752m above the original budget provision. More critically, annual incremental drift exposure (cost of staff moving up pay grades) has increased from £1.5m to £4m per annum. The CFO warns this will 'challenge the ongoing viability of numerous council services' because services must absorb this cost from their own budgets.
findings.matters: Pay costs are a structural budget driver. A tripling of incremental drift exposure that was not budgeted centrally means either services will under-deliver or further reserves will be drawn.
findings.figures: New pay structure: £4.545m permanent cost increase (2.44%). Over-budget by: £1.752m. Incremental drift: £1.5m → £4m per annum (167% increase).
findings.quote: the increase in base salary costs implemented via this project and the additional incremental drift will challenge the ongoing viability of numerous council services.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 10 - s25 CFO Reserves Strategy Report 202627
findings.headline: 2025/26 overspend of £4.6m forecast despite expenditure freeze; Adult Social Care already £3.8m over
findings.detail: Despite a freeze on non-essential expenditure and vacancies implemented from October 2025, the council is forecasting an in-year overspend of £4.6m (1.3% of budget). Adult Social Care is predicting a £3.8m (2.7%) overspend in 2025/26. This pattern is expected to continue: £7m of demand and inflationary growth is being provided for Children's Services alone in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Budget forecasts are not holding even with emergency expenditure controls in place. This signals either unrealistic budget setting or demand/cost pressures the council cannot manage within its resource envelope.
findings.figures: 2025/26 total overspend forecast: £4.6m (1.3% of net budget). Adult Social Care 2025/26: £3.8m (2.7%) overspend. 2026/27 Children's Services growth provision: £7m.
findings.quote: the Council is currently forecasting that it will overspend its 2025/26 approved budget by £4.6m (1.3% of its net budget) after the release of all the budgeted contingencies.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 10 - s25 CFO Reserves Strategy Report 202627
findings.headline: Unearmarked reserves falling to 6% of expenditure and CFO explicitly states they are inadequate
findings.detail: Unearmarked reserves are forecast to fall from £29.3m (8% of net revenue expenditure) at March 2025 to approximately 6% by March 2027, after drawing down £4.8m to balance the 2026/27 budget. The CFO explicitly concludes that 'the level of reserves cannot be considered adequate' and warns that at current levels they are 'only just sufficient to cover an unexpected single event such as a cyber-attack' with no capacity to absorb multiple risks.
findings.matters: When the CFO explicitly warns reserves are inadequate, the council has minimal buffer for any adverse event. A single shock (cyber attack, demand spike, income loss) would require drastic action.
findings.figures: March 2025: £29.3m unearmarked (8% of NRE). March 2027 forecast: 6% of NRE. CIPFA minimum: 5%. Risk assessment range (excluding DSG): £20.4m–£37.5m required.
findings.quote: the Director of Finance also concludes that the level of reserves cannot be considered adequate given a clear understanding by members and senior management

findings.paper_title: Appendix 10 - s25 CFO Reserves Strategy Report 202627
findings.headline: External auditor concluded the council is not financially sustainable
findings.detail: Grant Thornton's 2024/25 audit report concluded BCP Council 'remains under significant financial pressure and is not financially sustainable due to both the current cumulative, and growing, deficit on its Dedicated Schools Grant'. The auditor also noted the council lacks effective arrangements for securing Economy, Efficiency and Effectiveness due to the statutory direction remaining in place for SEND services.
findings.matters: An external auditor's adverse conclusion on financial sustainability is a key credit signal. This is not a management view but an independent professional judgment.
findings.figures: Key Recommendation 1 (KR1): Council must update DSG management plan, monitor cashflow impact on reserves, and increase reserves where possible.
findings.quote: The Council remains under significant financial pressure and is not financially sustainable due to both the current cumulative, and growing, deficit on its Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG).

findings.paper_title: Appendix 10 - s25 CFO Reserves Strategy Report 202627
findings.headline: DSG deficit growing £95m+ annually; accumulated deficit forecast £379m by 2028 with no government support yet committed
findings.detail: The council's SEND spending vastly exceeds government grants: £73.5m spent against £64.5m grant in 2025/26 (£9m shortfall), rising to £95.7m forecast spend in 2026/27. The deficit grows £95m+ annually. Although government will take responsibility for day-to-day costs from 1 April 2028, the historic and accruing deficits will be retained by the council. Government has not yet committed support for these retained deficits despite earlier promises to announce details.
findings.matters: This is the structural cause of the council's insolvency. It is not discretionary overspending but a statutory service deficit the council cannot control, with no funding solution in place.
findings.figures: 2025/26: spend £73.5m vs grant £64.5m (£9m shortfall). 2026/27: forecast £95.7m spend. Annual deficit growth: £95m+. Accumulated deficit forecast by March 2028: £379m. Current (March 2025): £183m.
findings.quote: At the end of the Statutory Override extension period BCP Council is currently forecast to have an accumulated deficit of around £379m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 10 - s25 CFO Reserves Strategy Report 202627
findings.headline: Council will breach its borrowing limits in 2027/28 when it runs out of cash to fund the DSG deficit
findings.detail: BCP Council is cashflowing the DSG deficit using treasury management headroom (timing differences in receipt and payment flows). Current estimates show this headroom will be exhausted by the end of 2027/28, at which point the Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) threshold will be breached. This is the point at which the council runs out of cash to continue paying SEND bills on behalf of the Department for Education.
findings.matters: This flags a specific timeline to insolvency: within 18 months the council will be unable to meet its day-to-day cash obligations without emergency government support or a fundamental change in the DSG situation.
findings.figures: Treasury management headroom exhaustion forecast: end 2027/28. Robust management of capital slippage has deferred this from end 2025/26.
findings.quote: it is unlikely that it will be fully exhausted until the 2027/28 financial year which is therefore the latest estimate of when the threshold on borrowing, referred to as its Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) is forecast to be breached.

findings.paper_title: Addendum - BCP Council EFS proforma 2627 060126
findings.headline: Council's recovery plan is entirely dependent on a future government announcement of DSG support, with no alternative position
findings.detail: When asked whether the council has an alternative option to EFS and/or additional council tax increase, the council's response is: "Not without an announcement from government of guaranteed support for its historic and accruing DSG deficit." Additionally, any government support is conditional: "any announcement by government in respect of support for historic and accruing deficits will not be made until the final local government finance settlement for 2026/27 is announced and even when it is it will be conditional on an approved Local SEND Reform Plan."
findings.matters: The council has no Plan B and no control over its recovery path; everything depends on government announcements and political decisions outside the council's control, creating significant execution risk for lenders
findings.figures: £6.9m capitalisation request contingent on council tax flexibility; £9.9m contingent on government DSG support
findings.quote: Not without an announcement from government of guaranteed support for its historic and accruing DSG deficit.

findings.paper_title: Addendum - BCP Council EFS proforma 2627 060126
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review will reduce the council's funding by almost £6m in 2028/29 compared to 2025/26 levels, worsening long-term sustainability
findings.detail: BCP Council has modelled the impact of the Fair Funding Review and found they will receive almost £6m less cash in 2028/29 than currently receiving in 2025/26. This structural funding reduction is particularly severe given the council expected funding to increase, particularly from social care grants, under the previous formula. This compounds the cyclical pressures from DSG and in-year overruns.
findings.matters: A £6m structural funding reduction in 2028/29 makes it harder for the council to return to sustainability even if DSG support is provided, indicating long-term affordability risk
findings.figures: Almost £6m reduction in funding between 2025/26 and 2028/29
findings.quote: Doc6. Is an excel summary document which demonstrates BCP Council will be receiving almost £6m less cash in 2028/29 than it is actually receiving in 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Addendum - BCP Council EFS proforma 2627 060126
findings.headline: Capital receipts financing plan has an £11m shortfall, forcing the council to either find additional asset sales or cut transformation spending
findings.detail: The council proposes to finance £21.7m of capitalised revenue expenditure from capital receipts, but their forecast capital receipts only total £10.7m by March 2029. They explicitly state: "the council will need to either identify further asset disposals to increase the balance from £10.7m to £21.7m or reduce the programmed expenditure." This reveals a significant gap in their financing plan.
findings.matters: The capital receipts gap indicates the council's transformation and invest-to-save programmes may need to be curtailed, or the council will need to rely on asset sales it cannot yet confirm
findings.figures: £21.7m capitalisation need vs £10.7m forecast capital receipts = £11m gap
findings.quote: Therefore, the council will need to either identify further asset disposals to increase the balance from £10.7m to £21.7m or reduce the programmed expenditure.

findings.paper_title: Addendum - BCP Council EFS proforma 2627 060126
findings.headline: In-year overspend has escalated from £4.2m (Q2) to £5.2m (Q3), and the council is implementing emergency spend controls
findings.detail: Q2 budget monitoring showed a £4.2m overspend forecast. Q3 reporting due 3 February 2026 shows this has grown to £5.2m. The council has implemented a freeze on all non-essential expenditure and a vacancy freeze from 1 October 2025. Despite these controls and mitigation strategies, the overspend is worsening, suggesting operational budget control issues beyond structural pressures.
findings.matters: The in-year overspend, combined with the DSG crisis and Fair Funding Review impact, shows the council is struggling to maintain control of its budget even with emergency restrictions in place
findings.figures: £4.2m Q2 2025/26 forecast, £5.2m Q3 2025/26 forecast
findings.quote: This indicates the council was forecasting that it's in-year predicted overspend would be £4.2m. Early indications from the quarter three report due to be presented to Cabinet on the 3 February 2026 is that the overspend will have grown to £5.2m

findings.paper_title: Addendum - BCP Council EFS proforma 2627 060126
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit has nearly tripled in two years and is forecast to exceed £350m by 2028, creating an existential threat to the council's finances
findings.detail: The DSG deficit grew from £63.5m (March 2024) to £113.3m (March 2025) to £183.1m (March 2026). At this rate of growth, the deficit will exceed £350m by March 2028. The council describes this as causing an "existential threat to the council's financial sustainability." This SEND cost explosion is the core driver of the entire EFS request and the 2.43% additional council tax increase.
findings.matters: A £183m deficit in one service area that's growing to £350m is unsustainable and indicates a structural problem that lenders would view as a critical risk to the council's viability
findings.figures: £63.5m (March 2024), £113.3m (March 2025), £183.1m (March 2026), forecast over £350m by March 2028
findings.quote: At the current rate of growth the deficit will be over £350m by 31 March 2028

findings.paper_title: Addendum - 202627 Budget Report Addendum 100226v2
findings.headline: Council tax increased by 6.74% to cover DSG-driven pressures, limiting future tax flexibility
findings.detail: The council is increasing council tax by 6.74% in 2026/27 (4.99% standard rate plus additional 1.75% flexibility granted by government, plus 2% social care precept). Even at this level it remains below neighbouring Dorset Council charges, but has now used government's additional flexibility, constraining future tax-raising options.
findings.matters: High council tax increases signal service pressures and residual taxpayer resistance; having used the exceptional flexibility, future deficits cannot be addressed through tax. Resident complaints about service quality at high tax levels create political pressure.
findings.figures: Band D council tax 2026/27: £1,980.46 (increase £125.05 or 6.74% from 2025/26); Dorset Council 2026/27 estimated £2,100.90
findings.quote: An increase of an extra 1.75% would generate an extra £4.951m in financial resources for the council from 2026/27 onwards. It should be highlighted that even with the extra increase our 2026/27 council tax will be below the £2,001.05 charged by Dorset Council in the current 2025/26 financial year

findings.paper_title: Addendum - 202627 Budget Report Addendum 100226v2
findings.headline: Unearmarked reserves drawn down £4.825m to balance budget, only avoided by committing new council tax revenue to services
findings.detail: The original budget required a £4.825m drawdown of unearmarked reserves to achieve a balanced budget in 2026/27. This was avoided only by applying the additional 1.75% council tax flexibility (£4.9m) directly to service funding rather than building reserves. This leaves the council with no additional reserve cover and commits future revenue in a tight funding environment.
findings.matters: Reserve buffers are critical for cash flow stability and managing in-year pressures; using new revenue to avoid drawdown signals tight positioning and limits flexibility to handle demand shocks.
findings.figures: Reserve drawdown avoided £4.825m; council tax increase extra 1.75% generates £4.951m; residual £126k assigned to contingency
findings.quote: In order to present a legally balanced budget for 2026/27 the Council was having to draw down £4.825m in unearmarked reserves... The proposal is this extra council tax revenue is used to support essential services and enable the 2026/27 budget to be put forward avoiding the need to draw down £4.825m on unearmarked reserves.

findings.paper_title: Addendum - 202627 Budget Report Addendum 100226v2
findings.headline: Council borrowing £95.7m for SEND deficit in 2026/27 based on temporary government assurance, not legal guarantee
findings.detail: The council is approved to borrow £95.7m to cover the SEND deficit revenue gap in 2026/27, justified by 'previous assurance from government that the council can exceed its borrowing thresholds temporarily'. This assurance is temporary and contingent on government commitment to SEND system reform; the government has not formally guaranteed it.
findings.matters: If government assurance is withdrawn or SEND reform stalls, the council cannot sustain this borrowing level; it would need immediate action to reduce spending or find alternative funding.
findings.figures: Borrowing £95.7m in 2026/27; estimated interest saving from deferred DSG deficit support £6.6m per annum from 2027/28 onwards
findings.quote: Agree to borrow £95.7m to fund the 2026/27 excess Special Educational Needs and Disability (SEND) High Needs DSG revenue expenditure above the government grant being made available. This is also based on previous assurance from government that the council can exceed its borrowing thresholds temporarily

findings.paper_title: Addendum - 202627 Budget Report Addendum 100226v2
findings.headline: Structural revenue funding gap of £18.1m by 2028 despite new revenue sources and DSG support
findings.detail: Even after the government's extra 1.75% council tax flexibility (generating £4.9m annually) and the assumed 90% DSG deficit support, the council faces an £18.1m funding gap over the medium term to March 2028. This is driven by declining Revenue Support Grant (RSG) falling by £5.9m per year, equating to £15m annual loss by 2028/29.
findings.matters: A structural gap this large signals future service cuts or further reserve depletion are inevitable; the council cannot close it through one-off measures.
findings.figures: Funding gap reduced from £30.1m to £18.1m by 2028 after all measures; RSG decline £5.9m per annum by 2028/29; gap for 2027/28 alone £6.9m
findings.quote: reduce the funding gap over the period to 31 March 2028 from £24.8m down to £18.1m with the funding gap for 2027/28 reducing from £13.6m to £6.9m

findings.paper_title: Addendum - 202627 Budget Report Addendum 100226v2
findings.headline: Government DSG support is conditional and not guaranteed, creating budget risk for 2026/27 and beyond
findings.detail: The £165.24m High Needs Stability Grant requires Department for Education approval of a Local SEND Reform Plan and will not be paid until autumn 2026. Further government support for deficits in 2026/27 and 2027/28 is acknowledged as discretionary and 'not unlimited'. If this support is not approved or reduced, the council's budget and medium-term plan collapse.
findings.matters: Budget delivery depends on discretionary government funding outside the council's control; non-approval would force immediate service cuts or further reserve depletion.
findings.figures: High Needs Stability Grant £165.24m (90% of £183.6m); further support for 2026/27 and 2027/28 deficits assumed but not quantified or guaranteed
findings.quote: This grant will be subject to BCP Council submitting and securing the Department for Education (DfE) approval of a Local SEND Reform Plan... it was recognised that this support would not be unlimited.

findings.paper_title: Addendum - 202627 Budget Report Addendum 100226v2
findings.headline: Council will remain technically insolvent despite historic DSG deficit support from government
findings.detail: The government's High Needs Stability Grant will cover 90% of the historic DSG deficit (£165.24m), but the council explicitly acknowledges it will still be technically insolvent because the remaining deficits exceed reserves. The council faces a locally-managed residual deficit of £37.9m from 2028/29 onwards, when the statutory override allowing DSG deficits to be ignored in accounts ends.
findings.matters: Technical insolvency signals structural financial stress that government support only defers rather than resolves; solvency risk is material for lenders and governance.
findings.figures: Historic deficit £183.6m as at 31 March 2026; government grant covers £165.24m (90%); residual deficit for local funding £37.9m from 2028/29
findings.quote: Although this contribution is welcome and positive the council will still be technically insolvent as these net deficits will still be greater than the councils' forecast reserves.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: 10-year gilt yields reached 27-year high of 5.6% in August, making council borrowing unusually expensive.
findings.detail: Long-dated gilts experienced pronounced sell-off in August, driven by investor concerns over fiscal consolidation and reduced demand from pension funds. While yields have since eased, the recent spike to 5.6% represents the highest in 27 years and reinforces cost of any borrowing undertaken in current market.
findings.matters: Lenders monitor gilt yields as proxy for all UK council borrowing costs; validates council's decision to defer borrowing until rates normalise.
findings.figures: 5.6% (10-year gilt); 22 basis points sell-off; 27-year high
findings.quote: During August, long-dated gilts underwent a particularly pronounced sell-off, climbing 22 basis points and reaching a 27-year high of 5.6% by the end of the month.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Council has £12.8m of past MRP overpayments available to reclaim for budget use if necessary.
findings.detail: Between April 2023 and March 2025, the council made voluntary revenue provision payments in excess of the statutory minimum. Policy allows reclamation of these overpayments if deemed prudent, creating a material financial reserve.
findings.matters: Represents significant discretionary reserves that could be deployed to address future budget pressures; shows prior financial conservatism that now provides flexibility.
findings.figures: £12.8m cumulative
findings.quote: The cumulative amount of VRP overpayments made between 1 April 2023 and 31st March 2025 was £12.8m.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 202627 241225
findings.headline: Council has forgone £12.4m per annum in council tax by choosing not to increase by permitted levels since reorganisation in 2019
findings.detail: BCP Council has deliberately set council tax increases below the government-permitted threshold since the 2019 unitary authority formation. The cumulative effect is that the council is now charging £12.4m per annum less than it could have raised, and is now 4.4% below where council tax would be if set at maximum permitted levels since 2019.
findings.matters: This is a policy choice that has directly constrained service capacity and reserves. It signals local political constraints on raising income that may persist even as financial pressure increases.
findings.figures: £12.4m per annum forgone income; BCP council tax £1,855.41 vs. £1,937.42 if harmonised and maximised since 2019 (4.4% shortfall)
findings.quote: We are therefore clear that this council has locally decided not to generate and therefore forfeit the £12.4m per annum extra revenue that we could have been generating. While this is an annual benefit to our local council taxpayers it will have had a direct impact on the level of services the council has been able to provide.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 202627 241225
findings.headline: SEND caseload is 13% higher year-on-year and timeliness for assessments declining despite statutory duties
findings.detail: EHCPs are growing 13.3% year-on-year (4,343 to 4,921 between Nov 2024 and Nov 2025). Timeliness for new assessments has declined to 52.8% against a 20-week target. The council is struggling to resource the service and has prioritised only the most vulnerable (elective home education, known to social care), effectively rationing a statutory duty.
findings.matters: Demand growth is outpacing funding growth and the council is choosing not to meet statutory timescales for all children. This increases reputational risk and legal challenge risk, and signals the DSG crisis is not stabilising.
findings.figures: 4,921 EHCPs November 2025 (13.3% growth YoY); 52.8% meeting 20-week timeliness; caseload 13% higher than prior year
findings.quote: The number of Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) continues to rise to 4,921 in November 2025 compared to 4,343 in November 2024 (3,683 in November 2023), representing a percentage increase of 13.3% since November 2024. It should be noted that the SEND service's caseload is now 13% higher than this point last year.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 202627 241225
findings.headline: Director of Finance states reserves are inadequate and cannot cover multiple simultaneous risks
findings.detail: The s25 formal advice states unearmarked reserves at 6% are insufficient for multiple risks and only just sufficient for a single event. The CFO explicitly advises that any such event would require drastic action to restore reserves to minimum levels, and reserves would be clearly insufficient for realisation of multiple risks.
findings.matters: This is formal statutory advice that the council's financial resilience is inadequate. It places liability with members for any adverse outcome, and signals to a lender that financial buffers are exhausted.
findings.figures: 6% unearmarked reserves as percentage of NRE; no buffer for multiple concurrent pressures
findings.quote: At around 6%, unearmarked reserves are only just sufficient to cover an unexpected single event such as a cyber-attack or significant in-year overspending. Any such single event would then require drastic action to restore such reserves to the minimum recommended level. They would clearly be insufficient for the realisation of multiple risks.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 202627 241225
findings.headline: Council applied for Exceptional Financial Support in January 2026 and is seeking permission to increase council tax beyond government threshold
findings.detail: BCP applied for government Exceptional Financial Support specifically requesting flexibility to increase council tax by more than the 4.99% threshold and permission to capitalise £10.5m of borrowing costs for the DSG deficit. This signals the council has exhausted conventional options and is requesting extraordinary measures.
findings.matters: An EFS application is an admission of financial failure. It also signals that government has not yet committed to support the DSG deficit, leaving the April 2028 cliff date unresolved.
findings.figures: £10.5m DSG borrowing costs sought for capitalisation; council tax flexibility requested
findings.quote: In response to a 6 January 2026 application by the Council for Exceptional Financial Support from the government. o Government permission to increase council tax by more than the 4.99% threshold limit. o Government permission to capitalise the £10.5m cost of borrowing to finance the DSG deficit in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 202627 241225
findings.headline: Significant funding gaps of £30m over 2027/28 and 2028/29 remain even after £15m of assumed savings
findings.detail: The medium-term financial plan shows funding gaps of £30m over the two-year period 2027/28 to 2028/29, even factoring in £15m of future savings. This means the council must identify an additional £7.5m per year in savings beyond what it has already committed to avoid further reserve drawdowns or service collapses.
findings.matters: The council has not yet identified or costed the savings required to balance 2027/28 and beyond. This is below the threshold of a credible medium-term plan and signals genuine financial distress ahead.
findings.figures: £30m funding gap over 2027/28–2028/29; £15m assumed savings = £15m unresolved gap
findings.quote: Significant funding gaps in future financial years amounting to £30m over the two year period 2027/28 and 2028/29. This is after £15m of assumed future savings over this same time period.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 202627 241225
findings.headline: 2025/26 budget already in £4.6m overspend (1.3% of net service budget) with quarter 4 still to come
findings.detail: The council is forecasting an in-year overspend of £4.6m for 2025/26, primarily driven by children's social care. The position has deteriorated from quarter 2 to quarter 3 by £0.4m. This overspend is to be funded from business rates collection fund surplus, further depleting the one-off resources available for 2026/27.
findings.matters: Current-year overspend signals inability to control core service costs in real time. This is children's social care—the most inflexible cost base—indicating demand is structural, not cyclical.
findings.figures: £4.6m overspend (1.3% of budget); deteriorated £0.4m from Q2 to Q3; attributable to children's social care
findings.quote: The December projection for the current 2025/26 financial year is that the council is currently forecasting that it will overspend its 2025/26 approved budget by £4.6m (1.3% of its net service budget) after the release of the budgeted contingencies. Overall, the position has deteriorated by £0.4m compared to the quarter two reported position and reflects the ongoing challenges facing local government from children's social care.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 202627 241225
findings.headline: Government funding falling in absolute terms: council will receive less cash in each of next three years than 2025/26, equivalent to £15m annual shortfall by 2028/29
findings.detail: Under the new Fair Funding Formula, BCP's rebased Settlement Funding Assessment declines from £145.4m (2025/26) to £139.5m (2028/29), a -4.1% reduction over three years. The report explicitly states BCP will be £15m worse off by 2028/29 if funding had merely kept pace with the government's own 2% inflation target.
findings.matters: Declining government funding cannot be compensated by service efficiency or council tax alone. The council faces a structural funding crisis independent of its own performance, with no recovery expected in the planning period.
findings.figures: SFA £145.437m (2025/26), £144.003m (2026/27), £141.539m (2027/28), £139.505m (2028/29); cumulative loss of ~£15m by year 3 versus inflation-adjusted baseline
findings.quote: On the basis that it would have been fair to assume the 2025/26 funding would have increased by at least the government's 2% inflationary target the indication is the council will be losing around £15m annually by the 3rd year (2028/29) of the settlement.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 202627 241225
findings.headline: Council is drawing £4.8m from unearmarked reserves to balance the 2026/27 budget, reducing them to 6% of NRE despite strategy to improve financial health
findings.detail: The Director of Finance explicitly states that using unearmarked reserves to balance this budget is contrary to the administration's strategy to improve financial health and sustainability. Reserves will fall from 8% of NRE (31 March 2025) to 6% (31 March 2027), leaving them barely above the 5% statutory minimum and insufficient to cover multiple simultaneous risks.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdown signals that the council cannot balance its budget from operational income. At 6%, a single major incident (cyber-attack, SEND cost spike, care case overspend) would exhaust reserves and force emergency service cuts.
findings.figures: £4.8m drawdown in 2026/27; reserves fall from 8% to 6% of NRE
findings.quote: It is intended to fund this forecast overspend from the one-off additional business rates resources being made available in 2026/27. The use of unearmarked reserves to balance this budget is contrary to the strategy of the Administration to improve the financial health and sustainability of the Council.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 202627 241225
findings.headline: DSG deficit is growing by £95.7m per year and forecast to reach £379m by March 2028, with council retaining all historic and accruing deficits
findings.detail: The high needs revenue expenditure deficit is forecast to grow from £73.5m in 2025/26 to £95.7m in 2026/27. The Chancellor announced government will take over SEND funding from April 2028, but the council will retain the current £113.3m deficit plus an additional £266m estimated to accumulate over three years. The council is borrowing £95.7m in 2026/27 to pay SEND bills it cannot fund from grant.
findings.matters: The council is accumulating an unsustainable structural deficit that cannot be resolved through savings or efficiency. Interest costs on SEND borrowing are eating into operational capacity, and the endpoint—April 2028—creates a cliff where either reserves must absorb £379m or government must provide support.
findings.figures: £73.5m gap (114% of grant) in 2025/26; £95.7m gap (148%) in 2026/27; £113.3m historic deficit + £266m accruing = £379m by 31/3/28; £10.5m annual interest cost in 2026/27
findings.quote: The predicted £73.5m annual funding gap for 2025/26 (114%) is forecast to grow to an annual funding gap of £95.7m (148%) in 2026/27

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 202627 241225
findings.headline: Council has been technically insolvent since April 2025 due to DSG deficit exceeding reserves, protected only by statutory override until March 2028
findings.detail: The accumulated DSG deficit at 31 March 2025 was £113.3m, greater than the council's total general fund reserves. This technical insolvency would normally require a Section 114 notice, but is currently masked by government legislation. When the statutory override expires on 1 April 2028, the council will face actual insolvency unless the deficit is resolved.
findings.matters: Statutory insolvency is the end state for councils in financial failure. A lender faces the risk that government may impose administration or that the council's ability to service debt could be compromised.
findings.figures: £113.3m DSG deficit as at 31/3/25; statutory override expires 31/3/28
findings.quote: From 31 March 2025 the council was technically insolvent as the DSG deficit was greater than the councils total general fund reserves. Ordinarily any council in this position would be required to issue what is referred to as a s114 report which would put the council into effective administration

findings.paper_title: Appendix 8 202627 Asset Management Plan (1)
findings.headline: Implementation of a new Corporate Landlord Model with a pilot centralising budgets from April 2025.
findings.detail: The council is transitioning from service-managed property to a centralized Corporate Landlord Model, consolidating strategic asset management, estates, facilities, compliance, repairs, maintenance, and design. A pilot centralizing budget approach is planned for April 2025, linking corporate register assets with associated costs in the finance system. Currently, not all financial costs can be linked to individual assets.
findings.matters: This structural change indicates asset management has been fragmented and costs not properly tracked. The audit weakness (inability to link costs to assets) is now being remedied, but the transition creates execution risk.
findings.figures: 2,620 asset entries on corporate asset register; over 10,000 HRA assets (separately managed); budget pilot planned April 2025
findings.quote: Pilot a centralised budget approach in April 2025 by linking corporate register assets with their associated costs in the finance system. Currently not all financial costs can be linked to individual assets

findings.paper_title: Appendix 8 202627 Asset Management Plan (1)
findings.headline: The council acknowledges unprecedented financial challenges and is using asset management to respond to them.
findings.detail: Section 10.1 directly states the council faces unprecedented financial challenges and that assets have a key role in responding. The strategy emphasizes continually challenging whether assets are required, fit for purpose, and whether the council can afford to maintain them. The corporate landlord model implementation is explicitly linked to delivering financial efficiencies and reducing revenue operating costs.
findings.matters: The council is explicitly signalling financial stress and restructuring asset management as a cost-control mechanism. This is a leading indicator of broader financial pressure beyond this plan.
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: The Council's assets have a key role to play regarding responding to the unprecedented financial challenges the Council faces over the next few years. Assets can directly affect both the revenue and capital positions of the Council.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 8 202627 Asset Management Plan (1)
findings.headline: The council has a substantial maintenance backlog and is managing buildings reactively due to budget constraints.
findings.detail: The document states maintenance budgets are focused only on ensuring statutory obligations are met. Buildings are being maintained on a reactive basis, and the council does not hold a full set of live condition information because budgets are stretched. Facilities management is prioritising only repairs that directly impact health and safety compliance and operational continuity.
findings.matters: A reactive maintenance regime with a backlog indicates future capital demand. Deferred maintenance can lead to sudden large costs, building failures, or service disruption. This is a material contingent liability.
findings.figures: Maintenance £9.89m current spend (2024-25); council maintains over 1,200 properties out of 2,300 sites owned
findings.quote: current resource constraints require prioritisation of repairs that directly impact health and safety compliance and to ensure that a service can operate from that site. While this approach ensures legal and compliance obligations are met, it does present a challenge between our broader goal of proactive estate management and the reactive focus on health and safety issues

findings.paper_title: Appendix 8 202627 Asset Management Plan (1)
findings.headline: The council's transformation programme costs are to be funded through asset disposals via Flexible Use of Capital Receipts.
findings.detail: Principle 1 of the disposal strategy explicitly commits to securing asset disposals to fully fund transformation programme costs. This is a material dependency: the transformation is dependent on achieving the required disposal receipts by 31 March each year. The council is progressing Phase 2 of Estates & Accommodation consolidation focused on administrative buildings.
findings.matters: Lenders need to know the council's transformation funding plan relies on achieving specific asset sale targets. Failure to dispose of assets at planned values or timing would create a capital funding gap.
findings.figures: £2.16bn total portfolio valuation (November 2025); Rates £6.9m, Utilities £7.5m, Maintenance £9.89m (2024-25); £22m Boscombe Town Deal commitment
findings.quote: We will ensure sufficient assets disposals are secured to enable the council's transformation programme costs to be fully funded by the Flexible Use of Capital Receipts. This will require disposal of assets where completion can be guaranteed by the 31 March of the relevant financial year

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring 2025-26 at Quarter three
findings.headline: Planning income continuing to decline, driving Operations directorate pressure
findings.detail: Planning income is identified as a main source of pressure within Operations services, continuing a trend from the prior year. This reduction in income contributes to the £0.608m Operations directorate overspend.
findings.matters: Sustained planning income decline suggests underlying weakness in the local economy and development activity that may persist, reducing a key council income source.
findings.figures: Operations directorate overspend £0.608m, with planning income reduction a key driver
findings.quote: Within operations services the main pressures are from reduced planning income (continuing the trend from last year), and additional costs for emergency repairs and cleaning costs in facilities management.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring 2025-26 at Quarter three
findings.headline: Earmarked reserves drawn down by £23.2m, reducing from £55.7m to £32.5m
findings.detail: Earmarked reserves are declining significantly from £55.7m to £32.5m, a drawdown of £23.2m through drawing down government grants and progressing corporate projects. Combined with the general fund overspend, this leaves the council with less financial flexibility.
findings.matters: Depleting reserves reduce the council's ability to absorb unexpected financial shocks or to invest in priority areas and indicate the council is drawing on reserves to fund ongoing operations.
findings.figures: Earmarked reserves £55.7m → £32.5m (movement -£23.2m); Total reserves £83.0m → £61.8m
findings.quote: The main movements in earmarked reserves include drawing down government grants in line with the latest profile of their application, progressing priority corporate and transition and transformation projects.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring 2025-26 at Quarter three
findings.headline: Specialist education provision for age 16-25 doubled year-on-year, driving unsustainable DSG cost growth
findings.detail: The paper reports significant growth in the number of children and adults up to age 25 in DfE-hosted specialist provisions over 2024-25, with the number in specialist post-16 institutions doubling. This placement surge drives the high needs funding pressure. The paper notes there is no indication yet that the special education needs improvement strategy is changing the trajectory of demand or reducing costs.
findings.matters: Doubling of specialist education placements indicates structural cost pressures the council cannot control and indicates the DSG deficit will continue to grow regardless of local spending discipline.
findings.figures: Specialist post-16 institutions numbers doubled over 2024-25; DSG high needs projected overspend £15.5m in 2025-26
findings.quote: The significant growth over 2024/25 in the number of children and adults up to age 25 in specialist provisions, with the number in specialist post-16 institutions doubling. There is no indication yet that the special education needs improvement strategy is changing the trajectory of demand or reducing the average cost of provision.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring 2025-26 at Quarter three
findings.headline: Capital programme £74m reprofiled to future years with only 42% spent to date
findings.detail: The capital programme was reduced from £173m at Q2 to £99m at Q3 due to £74m of schemes (including flood defences and Port of Poole) being reprofiled to future years. Spend to date is only 42% of the reduced programme, with particularly low spend in Operations and Children's Services.
findings.matters: Significant capital reprofiling and low spend rates indicate either cash constraints preventing investment, planning delays on major schemes, or scope issues, all of which affect the council's capacity to address service resilience.
findings.figures: Programme £136m (Feb) → £173m (Q2) → £99m (Q3); £74m reprofiled to future years; 42% spend rate at Q3
findings.quote: The total resources for the 2025/26 capital investment programme increased from the £136m agreed in February to £173m at quarter two but reduced to £99m in quarter three. This is due to capital scheme budgets of £74m reprofiled to future years. Spend to date is still relatively low at 42% of the reduced programme.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring 2025-26 at Quarter three
findings.headline: Adult social care experiencing £2.826m overspend from care cost inflation only partially mitigated
findings.detail: Care costs have increased in adult social care (Wellbeing directorate £2.826m overspend on net budget £137.963m), only partially offset by additional income and commissioning savings. This suggests cost inflation in care markets that the council is only partly able to mitigate.
findings.matters: Persistent care cost inflation combined with partial mitigation suggests ongoing structural cost pressures in social care that will not ease without demand or provision model changes.
findings.figures: Wellbeing directorate £2.826m overspend; net budget £137.963m
findings.quote: Care costs have increased in adult social care with offset from additional income and commissioning savings reducing the overall pressure from the last quarter.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring 2025-26 at Quarter three
findings.headline: Children's social care overspend of £5.11m due to growing caseload and higher placement costs
findings.detail: The Children directorate shows a £5.11m overspend (on a net budget of £100.083m). Pressures from new caseload and higher placement costs have continued to grow and remain unmitigated by budgeted savings.
findings.matters: Growing children's social care costs indicate structural demographic or assessment pressures that are not being controlled by the council's planned savings, and suggest similar pressures across local government will persist.
findings.figures: Children directorate £5.11m overspend; net budget £100.083m
findings.quote: The pressure in children's social care have continued to grow with new caseload and higher placement costs.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring 2025-26 at Quarter three
findings.headline: General fund overspend of £4.6m is worsening quarter-on-quarter despite releasing £2.8m contingency
findings.detail: The general fund overspend increased from £4.2m at Q2 to £4.6m at Q3, a deterioration of £0.4m. This persists after releasing the central general contingency of £2.8m, meaning underlying budget pressures are not being controlled. There is no specific contingency this year to counter non-delivery of programmed savings.
findings.matters: A growing in-year overspend suggests structural budget misalignment and indicates that without significant management action, the council will end the year with lower reserves than planned, reducing financial resilience.
findings.figures: Q3 overspend £4.6m vs Q2 £4.2m; general contingency released £2.8m; no contingency for savings non-delivery
findings.quote: The quarter three position is a projected overspend for the general fund of £4.6m (compared with £4.2m at quarter two) largely due to increased demand for adult and children social care. There is no specific contingency this year to counter non-delivery of programmed savings.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring 2025-26 at Quarter three
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant accumulated deficit projected to reach £183.6m, exceeding total council reserves of £61.8m
findings.detail: The DSG accumulated deficit is growing from £113.3m to £183.6m due to a £15.5m high needs overspend in 2025-26 plus a budgeted gap of £57.5m. This accumulated deficit now exceeds the council's total reserves, and the paper warns this will inevitably exhaust the council's cash position which is currently covering the high needs excess. The council is in conversations with MHCLG seeking immediate solution but outcome is not yet known.
findings.matters: A deficit this large that exceeds reserves indicates potential insolvency risk and means the council's cash flow is being drained to cover special education costs, directly impacting its financial sustainability and ability to weather other shocks or borrow.
findings.figures: Accumulated deficit £183.6m projected 31 March 2026 vs total reserves £61.8m; high needs overspend £15.5m; in-year funding gap £70.3m
findings.quote: The accumulated DSG deficit greater than the total of the council's earmarked and unearmarked reserves on 31 March 2025. The forecast that the in-year funding gap is continuing to grow will inevitably bring forward the date when the council exhausts its cashflow position.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Monitoring report for the period April to December 2025 and Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Council deliberately maintains high cash balances through short-term borrowing into April 2026, creating a refinancing point
findings.detail: Strategy is to borrow only cash needed through April 2026, keeping balances higher than structurally necessary to invest in the inter-Local Authority money market. This boosted treasury returns to 4.16% but all the short-term loans need refinancing or repayment at once in April 2026.
findings.matters: Concentrates refinancing risk into a single month; the strategy depends on continued availability and attractiveness of inter-Local Authority lending rates, and borrowing rates at that point. If credit conditions tighten or rates spike in Q1 2026, refinancing could be difficult or expensive.
findings.figures: Investment returns averaged 4.16% April-December 2025 vs SONIA 4.05%; inter-Local Authority strategy enabled £0.6m reduction in interest costs vs Q2 forecast
findings.quote: A strategy of borrowing cash required into April 2026 mean we have higher cash balances to invest in the short term and have been able to take advantage of the high interest rates being paid within the inter-Local Authority market.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Monitoring report for the period April to December 2025 and Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Accumulated DSG deficit is driving increase in short-term borrowing
findings.detail: Council's short-term debt has increased significantly since April 2022, with Table 6 explicitly overlaying accumulated DSG deficit against debt growth to show the connection. The document confirms short-term debt increases are specifically to satisfy cash demand from the DSG deficit.
findings.matters: DSG deficit is a structural funding gap with no grant covering the full cost of schools spending; this forces BCP into ongoing reliance on borrowing to bridge the gap, which absorbs credit capacity and reduces financial flexibility for other priorities.
findings.figures: Significant increase in short-term borrowing over April 2022 to December 2025 period; accumulated DSG deficit shown in Table 6
findings.quote: Debts in the short term have increased significantly to satisfy the cash demand of the deficit.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2024/25 Action Plan Update and Annual Review of Local Code of Governance
findings.headline: Central government has delayed providing detail on DSG deficit support that was expected in December 2025
findings.detail: Detail on support for councils with DSG deficits up to 2028/29 and conditions for accessing support were anticipated in the December 2025 Local Government Finance Settlement but are now being promised later in the process. This creates uncertainty around interim deficit recovery support and the council's borrowing plan.
findings.matters: Delayed clarity on government support increases uncertainty around the council's ability to service its growing DSG deficit and future borrowing requirements.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: Further detail on support for LAs with historic and accruing deficits, up to 2028/29, and conditions for accessing such support, were anticipated to be shared in the December 2025 provisional 2026/27 Local Government Finance Settlement. They are now being promised later in the settlement process.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2024/25 Action Plan Update and Annual Review of Local Code of Governance
findings.headline: Accumulated DSG deficit projected to reach £183.1m by March 2026, up from £113.3m in March 2025
findings.detail: The schools budget deficit is driven by high needs funding shortfalls of £44.6m in 2024/25 and £57.5m in 2025/26, partly due to out-of-borough placement costs. The council is using temporary borrowing to cover the 2025/26 shortfall, contingent on central government delivering promised SEND funding reform.
findings.matters: A £183m accumulated deficit materially affects the council's financial sustainability and borrowing capacity, and depends on central government delivering promised funding solutions.
findings.figures: £113.3m accumulated deficit (31 March 2025); £183.1m projected (31 March 2026); £44.6m annual shortfall 2024/25; £57.5m annual shortfall 2025/26
findings.quote: The DSG deficit continues to increase, with an accumulated DSG deficit of £113.3m as of 31 March 2025. This is predicted to grow to £183.1m by the 31 March 2026.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Monitoring update for Quarter 2 2025/26
findings.headline: Council achieving £300k interest underspend by accessing local authority market borrowing at rates lower than budgeted PWLB rates
findings.detail: The council's treasury strategy is delivering cost savings through opportunistic access to the local authority borrowing market, which provided rates lower than the short-term PWLB borrowing assumed in the budget. This demonstrates active debt cost management and financial flexibility in accessing competitive lending.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand a council's access to competitive borrowing markets and its ability to manage debt costs effectively, as this reflects market confidence and financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £300k underspend on interest payable budgets
findings.quote: The current forecast is an underspend of £300k on interest payable budgets. This is due to greater availability of funds within the local authority market than expected, this market provides lower rates compared to short term PWLB borrowing used to forecast borrowing costs.
